headline: Hi, I'm *Vlad*.
tagline: From writing code to designing systems

paragraphs: 7+ years building frontends people rely on every day: live betting odds, patient records, shift schedules for frontline teams.
Over the years, I've worked across sports betting, social platforms, healthcare, and enterprise workforce management.

This isn't my CV. It's the story of the problems that changed how I think, in about 5 minutes. I want to show how I grew as an engineer — from learning the fundamentals of JavaScript and React, to owning critical modules, making architectural decisions, working with large-scale systems, and thinking about stability and users.

transition: Every journey starts somewhere. For me, it started with vanilla JavaScript.

title: Capital Holding
subtitle: Frontend Developer · April 2019 — October 2020

paragraphs: My first position as a frontend developer. The product was a real-time betting platform — a high-frequency dashboard showing live sports events with data that never stopped moving.
It was the first time I had to understand how a real application is built — not just how to write code, but how different pieces work together.

cards.title: Project #1 — Vanilla JavaScript
cards.description: A sports betting platform built from scratch. No framework, just JavaScript.
cards.detail: That gave me a strong foundation in how the browser, application logic, data and UI work together — what happens underneath the abstractions frameworks would later provide.

cards.title: Project #2 — React + Redux
cards.description: The first project ended and a new betting platform began — this time with React and Redux.
cards.detail: I didn't want to simply learn the APIs. I wanted to understand why these tools existed, how state should flow through an application, and how to structure a growing frontend.

transition: I had learned how to build applications. Next, I had to learn how to build them with other people.

title: DataMix
tagline: The first time I understood that engineering is a team sport.
subtitle: Frontend Engineer · October 2020 — December 2021

paragraphs: My first outsourced experience — a product studio taking projects from MVP all the way to enterprise scale.
It was also the first place where I experienced a genuinely warm engineering environment. That mattered more than I expected.
Instead of staying on one product, I worked across different projects, domains and requirements — and grew from junior to a strong mid-level engineer in about a year and a half.

transition: Different domains, different constraints. Two projects taught me the most.

title: DataMix
tagline: The projects that taught me the most.
subtitle: Investment matching · Social network MVP

cards.title: Investment Matching Platform
cards.description: Core developer on a high-load two-sided marketplace connecting investors and investees.
cards.detail: Complex calculations, matching logic and large amounts of data taught me that frontend performance isn't only about rendering quickly — it's about how you structure data, state and the flow of information.

cards.title: Social Network (MVP)
cards.description: Sole frontend developer. Instagram-like platform, from scratch to MVP in six months.
cards.detail: Architecture, state, data fetching, UI, fluid animations, a multi-directional slider, performance and deployment. There was nobody to pass a frontend problem to.

blocks.heading: Engineering is more than writing code
items: It's helping another engineer solve a problem.
It's deciding whether something should become reusable.
It's thinking about how a technical decision affects the user and the client.
It's refactoring something even when nobody asks you to.

blocks.text: That's when I started seeing frontend engineering as a responsibility, not just a job.

transition: My questions were changing. "How should we build this?"

title: REMED
tagline: When I stopped thinking in screens.
subtitle: Frontend Engineer · December 2021 — August 2024

paragraphs: A healthcare CRM connecting doctors, clinics, laboratories and healthcare workflows with external healthcare systems.
It integrated with Helsi and Ukraine's national eHealth system, and contained some of the most heavily used modules I'd worked with up to that point.
blocks.quote: I wasn't implementing features anymore. I was responsible for parts of the system.

transition: The product was big. My part of it finally had edges — this is what owning it looked like.

title: REMED
subtitle: What I was responsible for

cards.title: High-load modules
cards.description: Doctor Workplace, Cashier Workplace and Calendar — doctor availability, appointments and patient data.

cards.title: Modular architecture
cards.description: Services, components, data storage and API layers organised per business entity.

cards.title: Cypress E2E testing
cards.description: Unit tests couldn't protect these journeys, so we covered the workflows people depended on.

cards.title: Mentoring
cards.description: Teaching juniors meant understanding things well enough to explain not only how, but why.

blocks.text: The best solution usually appeared somewhere between design, frontend and backend.

transition: I was thinking about ownership, boundaries and reliability. Then everything got bigger.

title: WorkJam
tagline: The most complicated frontend environment I'd worked in.
subtitle: Senior Frontend Engineer · March 2024 — July 2026

paragraphs: A frontline workforce platform — task management, scheduling, communication, learning and compliance for deskless teams in retail, hospitality, manufacturing and healthcare.
Multiple applications. Legacy Angular. Modern React and Next.js. Shared packages. Micro-frontends. A large monorepo. Multiple teams. And real users depending on the system every day.
When an application is already in production, "make it work" isn't enough. You have to think about stability, migration paths, backward compatibility, user experience and business impact.
I worked with the micro-frontend architecture that allowed React modules to be injected into legacy Angular applications while functionality gradually moved toward reusable shared packages.
blocks.quote: It wasn't a rewrite. It was a migration.

title: WorkJam · Case Study
eyebrow: Replacing flag infrastructure with zero downtime
tagline: How do you replace infrastructure without users noticing?

paragraphs: The platform relied heavily on Flagr and also used LaunchDarkly for feature management — two systems, years of accumulated tech debt, and every product depending on them.
We wanted to move to Harness Feature Management Engine. The challenge wasn't implementing Harness.
blocks.quote: The challenge was removing the old systems without disrupting production.

steps.label: Observe production, collect edge cases, iterate

blocks.text: Zero downtime. No service disruption. The migration happened while the platform kept serving users.
Planning a risky migration? I've done this before.

title: WorkJam · Case Study
tagline: Sometimes the best engineering decision is the one that saves two weeks.

paragraphs: We needed to add an agenda view to an existing calendar. The requirements sounded straightforward:

blocks.heading: The date picker problem
paragraphs: But the existing API wasn't designed around this experience, and we were working under a tight deadline.
The common component library didn't support the new design. The obvious solution was to create another component — and that meant a long tail of work:
Instead, I spent about two days researching the current implementation and found a way to extend it rather than duplicate it — leaving the platform with one date picker instead of two.

blocks.text: Delivered in around 10 days — 2 days of research saved ~2 weeks of building and a second component to maintain forever. The important part wasn't writing code faster — it was solving the right problem.

paragraphs: The platform consisted of four module applications and one unified application, and we needed to integrate them with Microsoft Teams.
The interesting part wasn't simply receiving Teams context. The challenge was preserving context while moving between independently running applications.
I created a reusable integration library that centralized Teams configuration, exposed a single way to read Teams context, and provided consistent cross-application navigation.
When a user clicked a link from Teams, the correct application instance had to open rather than navigating inside the current one — carrying context and state across the boundary.
blocks.quote: Solve the integration once. Make every application benefit from it.

blocks.text: Result: 1 library, 4 apps integrated, no copied Teams logic.

title: WorkJam · Case Study
eyebrow: One experience across web and native
tagline: When web and native have to become one experience.

paragraphs: We needed to bring a web chat experience into an Android application.
The module couldn't simply be bundled natively: Google's 4KB page-size requirement made that impossible. So we used WebView, keeping the native app lightweight.

Embedding the web application was only the beginning. Users were already authenticated in the native app, so they should never see a login screen. The web experience also needed native capabilities such as video recording and screenshots.

I implemented a JavaScript-to-native bridge — extending the global window object with methods the Android layer could call and respond to — so the web module could receive authentication context and reach Android APIs.
blocks.quote: The user shouldn't need to know which part of the product is native and which part is web.

blocks.text: Result: no second login, native video and screenshots from a web module, app size unchanged.

title: How I Think About Engineering
tagline: The technology changed. The questions changed more.
subtitle: What 7+ years of frontend engineering taught me

items: JavaScript taught me how the browser works.
React taught me how to structure interfaces.
Working across projects taught me how to collaborate.
Ownership taught me to think beyond individual features.
Large-scale systems taught me about boundaries, migration and reliability.

paragraphs: Somewhere along the way I stopped asking "How do I implement this?" and started asking:
blocks.quote: "What is the simplest system that lets us keep changing this?"

transition: The answers changed as the systems got bigger. A few things didn't.

title: Principles
tagline: The things that survived every stack I worked in.
subtitle: Six ideas I keep coming back to

cards.title: Clear boundaries
cards.description: Complex systems become easier to change when responsibilities are clearly separated.

cards.title: Simple code
cards.description: Enterprise software doesn't have to mean complicated software.

cards.title: Ownership
cards.description: If you own a module, you should understand its users, constraints, dependencies and failure modes.

cards.title: Pragmatism
cards.description: The newest technology isn't always the answer. Sometimes improving what exists is the better decision.

cards.title: Stability
cards.description: A production system is not a playground. Every change has users behind it.

cards.title: Collaboration
cards.description: Good engineering decisions rarely happen in isolation.

title: What's Next?
tagline: Got a frontend that's hard to change? That's my favourite kind of problem.
subtitle: Remote or hybrid · Wrocław, Poland

paragraphs: I do my best work when I own an area end to end: its users, its architecture, its failure modes — influencing architectural decisions and working alongside talented engineers.
I believe enterprise platforms can be written with clear and simple code. The key is setting clear boundaries and responsibilities between modules.

cards.title: Technical challenges
cards.description: High-load modules, performance problems and systems that require real technical thinking.

cards.title: Ownership

cards.title: Growth
